title: Learning to measure the air.
summary: A student-built wind tunnel, dry-ice flow visualization, and a measurement stand taking shape.

Sensor calibration, mounting geometry, repeatable conditions, and an uncertainty estimate remain necessary. Numerical design requirements and acceptance thresholds have not yet been supplied. Air is blown into that setup, and an outlet fan draws it through the tunnel.** The new stand uses differential pressure, load cells for lift and drag, and a BME280 for environmental conditions. The exact pressure-sensor model remains unconfirmed. Repeated smoke-system setbacks prompted a change in visualization method. Rithika proposed dry ice. The stand must also balance mechanical support with interference in the flow; that trade-off is still open. The earlier Arduino code contains a modeled differential-pressure channel with simulated noise and conditioning. It is an inspectable software artifact. Updated stand CAD and source will be added to GitHub later; existing files remain the linked evidence. **Proposed next procedure:** document the final stand and wiring; calibrate each force channel against a known reference; establish zero and repeatability; record ambient conditions; then define controlled comparison runs. This is a planning outline, not a performed experiment or an approved calibration protocol. Rithwik reports that the dry-ice setup produces a smooth visible flow into the inlet. This is a qualitative build observation. **No measured aerodynamic results or completed calibration records have been supplied.** The available CSV rows below are software sample input only. The original smoke approach required repeated changes to materials, filaments, air pumps, and the setup. The shift to dry ice in water is the documented response. A dated run-by-run failure log and photographs are still needed to make those iterations reproducible. Repository code, 3MF archives, and embedded previews can be inspected. Physical accuracy is not established by those files. Outstanding evidence includes updated wiring and stand CAD, calibration records, repeat trials, reference measurements, and an uncertainty budget. The latest stand is unfinished. No completed airfoil/aircraft mounting model, exact new pressure-sensor part number, flow-uniformity map, or force dataset has been supplied. The GitHub record predates the latest reported hardware configuration. The documented iteration separates making a phenomenon visible from measuring it. The change in visualization method solved a reported practical obstacle; reliable force measurement remains the next learning task. More detailed personal reflections can be added as they are recorded. Finish the stand and measurement chain, characterize the empty tunnel, and reproduce a NACA 0018 baseline before selecting a novel question. The [guided research plan](../../research/guided-aerodynamics-plan/) records the current stage gates, decision rules, and the evidence required before a dynamic experiment. title: From a signal to a useful record.
summary: CSV plotting and an offset-correction prototype for inspecting environmental data.
text: How do we make collected sensor data inspectable without confusing correction with calibration? Python CSV Flask Arduino The Python grapher reads environmental channels and creates plots. A separate Flask prototype explores offset correction, summary statistics, and CSV export. These tools support the wind-tunnel project. A record is easier to question when its raw values, units, and transformations stay visible. Plotting is part of inspection; it is not proof of sensor accuracy. Keep raw and transformed data distinct. Preserve timestamps and units. The Flask prototype requires its own runtime and is linked as source; it does not run on GitHub Pages. The earlier firmware schedules CSV records every two seconds. That is a configured interval, not a benchmark. A separate correction tool makes offsets inspectable but risks implying accuracy if calibration records are absent. The earlier modeled pressure channel includes noise and conditioning. Default offsets in the correction prototype are not treated as measured calibration coefficients. Source files for the logger, grapher, and correction tool exist in the linked repository. The current website provides a lightweight viewer for the exact three-row sample fixture. For the website viewer, reproduce the existing CSV values exactly, preserve units, and expose a table alongside the chart. No smoothing, extrapolation, or inference is applied. No dated software failure log is present in the reviewed record. The available limitation is the absence of independent calibration evidence for default offsets. The website checks that chart coordinates and table values reproduce the supplied fixture. This verifies display behavior only; it does not validate the original instruments or research software. Only three sample rows are available. Runtime testing of the original Flask/Python tools and verification of sensor accuracy are outside the evidence currently supplied. A corrected number needs a reason. Publish raw datasets, a calibration procedure, units, uncertainties, and source versions with future experiments.

title: A surprising signal is not yet a result.
summary: The Caltech conversations turned characterization into the first experiment: map the flow, test the sensors, and rule out vibration before calling a force trace aerodynamic.
text:
Instrumentation Uncertainty Experimental design ## Research objective

Learn to distinguish an aerodynamic phenomenon from an instrument artifact before attempting a dynamic experiment.

The 5 November conversation with a Caltech researcher made this the organizing rule for the next stage. A novel-looking signal is not evidence until the measurement system, the structure, and the software have each been tested as possible sources. The point is not to become suspicious of every result. It is to make the alternatives inspectable.

## Three possible sources of one trace

| Source | What it can look like | Evidence needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aerodynamic | Separation, shear-layer motion, finite-span loading, unsteady force | Repeatable dependence on flow speed, angle, and geometry, with a plausible mechanism |
| Mechanical | Mount resonance, bracket vibration, fan excitation, sensor cross-axis load | Zero-flow and motor-only tests, stiffness checks, impact or frequency-response tests |
| Software | Stuck-at-zero sensor, dropped sample, wrong unit, silent failure handling | Reference checks, range tests, timestamp checks, explicit invalid-value states |

The researcher described a reinforcement-learning experiment that appeared to converge because faulty sensors returned zero readings, which the software interpreted as zero error. They also described how an apparent force oscillation in a hypothetical airfoil/shear-layer experiment could come from a resonance of the mounts, brackets, or supports rather than from the flow. Neither example proves that this tunnel has the same fault. Together they show why the fault must be ruled out before the phenomenon is named.

## What to measure before measuring forces

The immediate recommendation was to map the velocity field first:

- Measure at the centerline and near the corners and edges of the test section.
- Move a single sensor through a grid if a sensor array is unavailable.
- Repeat the map at several stable fan or PWM settings.
- Record ambient temperature and pressure with the velocity observations.
- Document sampling duration, grid spacing, stabilization time, and repeat count instead of leaving them arbitrary.
- Measure the relation between PWM command and actual test-section velocity, then fit it with residuals. Any approximately linear behavior must be verified on this assembled tunnel, not assumed from a fan datasheet.
- Repeat conditions across runs, not only within one run.

This turns the empty tunnel into the first experiment. It also produces the reference needed to assign a Reynolds number. A fan's rated flow rate or duty cycle does not establish the velocity in the test section.

The researcher introduced shear layers as gradients in flow speed transverse to the main direction, with mixing and vortical motion as possible consequences. That is a phenomenon worth understanding. It is not evidence that the present tunnel has generated one.

## The dynamic experiment gate

A moving-angle-of-attack test adds four requirements at once:

1. A controlled, repeatable motion with a measured angle history.
2. Force, angle, speed, and environmental data on a common timeline.
3. Enough sensor bandwidth to resolve the expected force change.
4. A mount stiff enough that its resonances are outside, or clearly separable from, the frequency range of interest.

Before committing to a dynamic-pitch investigation, the apparatus needs zero-airflow force baselines, motor-only vibration records, a mount-stiffness assessment, sensor cross-axis checks, and a timing test. If those checks cannot separate a structural oscillation from an aerodynamic one, the experiment is not ready. A static finite-span or measurement-method comparison may be the stronger next study.

## Sensor failure is a data problem too

One practical lesson is easy to postpone: a disconnected or failed sensor must not become a plausible zero. The data pipeline should mark out-of-range values, detect a channel that never changes, preserve raw readings, and make dropped samples visible. A calibration record should include the reference, the date, the expected range, the observed offset or drift, and the units.

This is also a software requirement. A smooth plot is not proof that the values behind it are meaningful.

## Mentorship, with limits

The follow-up conversation confirmed that the Caltech researcher would serve as a PCIS mentor at roughly one hour of contact per month, subject to a busy schedule and possible rescheduling. They offered conceptual feedback and some possible access to surplus equipment. They did not promise sustained hands-on experimental supervision, regular code review, laboratory placement, authorship, or a recommendation.

The mentor supported aiming high while making clear that a peer-reviewed publication is uncertain given time and resources. Their advice was to choose a question worth sustaining because the learning matters even if the most ambitious publication goal is not reached. They discussed several directions, including wind prediction, aerodynamics, and propulsion, but did not select the final topic.

Public-facing names, titles, and approval to attribute the conversations are still to be confirmed. The mentoring arrangement should be documented separately from technical supervision, authorship, or institutional sponsorship.

## What changed

The earlier plan treated the stand as the next build milestone and the airfoil test as the next experiment. The revised order is stricter:

1. Finish and document the instrument.
2. Characterize the empty tunnel.
3. Validate a NACA 0018 baseline.
4. Only then choose a novel question.

The 2 November conversations supplied the research logic. The 5 November conversation supplied the measurement scepticism. Both are now part of the same gate.

## Next steps

- Write the empty-tunnel velocity-grid protocol with explicit grid, sampling, stabilization, and repeat rules.
- Test sensor-failure handling before collecting a dataset.
- Build the zero-flow and motor-only force records.
- Measure the actual PWM-to-speed relation, with residuals.
- Bring the characterization results and three technical questions to the next mentor meeting.
- Keep the dynamic experiment conditional until its mechanical and temporal response is measured.

## Revision record

**5 November 2026:** Created from the Caltech researcher conversations. No force or velocity dataset was supplied.

**6 November 2026:** Edited for publication with the revised research plan and the 2 November validation note.

title: A tunnel is not yet an instrument.
summary: Two conversations shifted the project from building a tunnel to earning the right to interpret it: validate NACA 0018 first, then look for a question the literature has not answered.
text:
Research design Validation Low-Reynolds number ## Research objective

Decide what the wind tunnel is for before asking it for a result. The tunnel is already a useful build. The harder question is whether it can become an instrument that produces evidence another person could inspect and repeat.

The 2 November review brought together two conversations: one with Scott, whose research has moved through experimental combustion, computational fluid dynamics, mathematical modeling, dynamics and control, and multi-agent systems; and one with an aerospace researcher at Texas A&M. They approached the problem from different directions and arrived at the same boundary between engineering and research.

## What changed

A working tunnel is not automatically a validated scientific instrument. Rebuilding a familiar NACA result can be excellent training, but the result is not automatically a contribution.

Scott's test was direct: read the literature, identify an unresolved question, and design the measurement around it. The Texas A&M researcher made the same distinction experimentally: first show that the apparatus can reproduce published lift and drag behavior at a comparable Reynolds number. Only then use the apparatus to probe something less characterized.

That reorders the project:

1. Establish what the tunnel actually produces.
2. Reproduce a known baseline.
3. Choose a question that survives a focused literature review.
4. Attempt the original experiment.

The interviews did not supply a research question that is already known to be novel. They supplied a procedure for deciding whether one is worth pursuing.

## What the conversations agreed on

| Guidance | Consequence for this project |
| --- | --- |
| A familiar result is not automatically new. | The NACA 0018 comparison is validation, not the final paper. |
| A research contribution needs a literature-defined gap. | No novelty claim until comparable sources have been read and recorded. |
| Low-Reynolds-number measurements are sensitive and hard to reproduce. | Agreement with a suitable reference would itself be a meaningful result. |
| Lift and drag need distinct, properly arranged force measurements. | A single ambiguous force channel is not enough for coefficient curves. |
| Advanced optics are not the first step. | PIV is not feasible here; the first task is credible velocity and force measurement. |
| The mechanism matters more than the software stack. | Each measurement should connect to an aerodynamic quantity, an assumption, and an uncertainty. |

The Texas A&M researcher also described particle image velocimetry as an advanced method well beyond the present budget. That was not a reason to avoid measurement. It was a reminder that even an expensive technique depends on experiment design, calibration, data handling, and an answerable question.

## The validation target

The working airfoil choice is NACA 0018. The proposed sequence is to hold angle of attack fixed, record the actual flow speed and ambient conditions, and compute lift and drag coefficients using documented reference dimensions. The results would then be compared with published data at the closest achievable Reynolds number and test geometry.

The comparison is not a formality. The eventual report would need to explain differences caused by flow non-uniformity, finite-span and end effects, blockage, mounting interference, force-system cross-talk, alignment, surface condition, or measurement noise. A disagreement could be more informative than a tidy curve if the cause is investigated honestly.

Several inputs are still missing. The test-section size has been described verbally as “8 by 8,” but the units and actual dimensions are unconfirmed. An approximate Reynolds-number range of 50,000 to 100,000 has been discussed, but it is based on fan specifications and informal estimates. It is not a measured operating range. The fan setting does not establish the velocity in the assembled test section; the velocity has to be measured.

## The literature problem

Scott cautioned that conventional two-dimensional NACA behavior has been studied extensively. He suggested looking beyond a repetition of that result toward finite-wing and three-dimensional effects, moving or morphing geometry, transient forces, or applications such as quieter propellers and rotors. Those were brainstorming directions, not verified gaps.

The Texas A&M conversation added rapid changes in angle of attack as a candidate: the force during motion can differ from the force at the same angle held steady, and the rate of motion may itself be a variable. Reverse-flow airfoil behavior, motivated by advancing and retreating rotor-blade conditions, was offered as another possible direction. Again, neither suggestion came with a literature review.

That leaves a clear task before any novel experiment: find out what has already been measured, under which conditions, and with what uncertainty. A direction becomes a research question only after that work.

## The provisional question

The plan now points toward a question that combines the interviews but remains unproven:

> At a measured low Reynolds number, how does the rate of change of angle of attack alter the time-dependent lift response of a finite NACA 0018 wing relative to fixed-angle baselines?

This is a candidate, not a final hypothesis. It is only credible if the apparatus can resolve the expected signal. Force-sensor bandwidth, dynamic mount stiffness, actuation, sampling, calibration, and synchronization all have to be tested first. If they cannot separate an aerodynamic response from mechanical vibration, a static finite-span or measurement-method study may be the more honest investigation.

## What this note establishes

The project now has two tracks that must not be confused:

- **Validation:** can the apparatus reproduce a known NACA 0018 result under documented conditions?
- **Contribution:** after the literature review, is there a specific unanswered question this apparatus can address?

The first track is executable now. The second remains a decision, not a promise. A peer-reviewed publication is an aspiration, not a guaranteed deliverable.

## Next steps

- Measure the tunnel and test-section geometry, and record the units.
- Find published NACA 0018 data at the closest achievable Reynolds number, aspect ratio, surface condition, and test method. Read each source before citing it.
- Document lift and drag as separate force channels with a calibration and alignment plan.
- Write the fixed-angle baseline protocol before running the first coefficient sweep.
- Review the dynamic-pitch literature and the apparatus requirements separately. Do not let one substitute for the other.

## Revision record

**2 November 2026:** Created from the first research-planning conversations. No measurements, coefficients, or novelty claims were added.

**6 November 2026:** Edited for publication alongside the revised research plan and the 5 November instrumentation note.

title: Before the plot, calibrate the measurement.
summary: What remains to be established before a corrected sensor value can support an aerodynamic claim.
text:
Instrumentation Uncertainty ## Research objective

Separate a useful plot from a defensible measurement. The current stand needs a way to connect sensor readings to known reference values before those readings can support force measurements.

## Background research

The earlier correction prototype contains default offsets. Subtracting an offset changes a number; a reference comparison is needed to justify the correction. The Arduino source also includes a modeled pressure channel with simulated noise and conditioning.

## Proposed method

This is a planning note. Document a reference, collect repeat readings at known conditions, record zero behavior and drift, then evaluate how the response changes across the intended range. Keep the raw observations alongside any fit or correction.

## Technical context

For a flow with density $\rho$ and speed $V$, dynamic pressure is:

$$q = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^2$$

If a suitable measurement establishes dynamic pressure, the corresponding relation is:

$$V = \sqrt{\frac{2q}{\rho}}$$

These are general relations, not results from this tunnel. Applying them requires an appropriate pressure arrangement, density assumptions, and a calibrated measurement. A generic differential-pressure sensor reading is not automatically dynamic pressure.

## Data and observations

No reference-calibration dataset has been supplied. No coefficients, fit quality, or uncertainty values are asserted here.

## What could go wrong

Mounting interference, zero drift, cross-axis sensitivity, incorrect units, or treating a modeled input as a physical reading could all undermine an interpretation. These are proposed checks, not observed failures of this stand.

## What this note establishes

The question is not whether software can draw a smooth line. It is whether the value on that line can be traced to a documented measurement process.

## Next steps

Choose and document reference checks for each channel once the stand geometry is settled. Record assumptions and uncertainty before reporting aerodynamic conclusions.

title: Three rows, and what they can actually tell us.
summary: Inspecting the exact sample input used by the environmental-data grapher, without treating it as an experiment.
text:
Python Data analysis ## Research objective

Inspect the input format used by the Python environmental-data grapher. The existing sample contains three rows dated 4 March 2026. They are example input, not wind-tunnel results.

## Software

The repository includes a Python grapher and a separate Flask correction prototype. This fieldbook's viewer displays the supplied rows without smoothing or extrapolation.

## Method

Read each channel with its unit. Preserve the source values. Plot elapsed minutes on the horizontal axis and one selected channel on the vertical axis. Make the underlying table available beside the chart.

```python
# Illustrative inspection of the repository sample format.
# This snippet is educational, not a quoted project implementation.
import csv

with open("sample.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as source:
    for row in csv.DictReader(source):
        print(row)
```

## Data and analysis

The sample temperature values are 23.4, 23.5, and 23.6 °C. Humidity is 41.2, 41.0, and 40.9 %. Pressure is 1008.6, 1008.7, and 1008.8 hPa. These values demonstrate the file format. Three sample rows cannot establish an environmental trend or aerodynamic result.

## What could go wrong

A plot can look authoritative even when its input is only a fixture. The viewer therefore carries a persistent “Sample input only” label and a direct source link. Changing the chart type does not change the evidence status.

## What this note establishes

Data display and measurement validation are separate tasks. A faithful visualization preserves provenance, units, and limitations along with the numbers.

## Next steps

When actual experiments produce datasets, add the acquisition method, instrument configuration, calibration record, repeat runs, and uncertainty information to the same content structure.

title: Reading a honeycomb, one layer at a time.
summary: A print archive contains more than a thumbnail. The extrusion moves reveal the honeycomb layer itself.
text:
Fabrication Geometry ## Research objective

Expose the geometry recorded in the current honeycomb print archive without pretending it is a flow simulation.

## Source material

The repository contains four sliced 3MF archives: two honeycomb files, a holder, and support corners. The source record does not establish which archived versions were fabricated in the later build.

## Method

The existing visualization was reconstructed from `Metadata/plate_1.gcode` in `honeyComb_Current.gcode.3mf`. It uses 3,724 positive-extrusion XY line segments in the slice whose `Z_HEIGHT` is 10 mm. Travel-only moves are omitted.

Coordinates were mapped uniformly into a 600 × 540 illustration and rounded to 0.1 display units. The preview in the archive showed a solid slab; the layer trace reveals the honeycomb infill.

## Observations

The image is a digital fabrication artifact. Its paths are evidence of instructions in the archive, not a photograph of a printed part, a dimensioned manufacturing drawing, or a measured flow field.

## Analysis and limitations

Filenames alone do not explain why a design changed. A layer trace also cannot establish how accurately a printer reproduced the part or how the finished honeycomb affects the flow.

## What this note establishes

A source artifact becomes more useful when a reader can inspect both the rendering and the original file. The caption is part of the evidence: it defines what the image can and cannot show.

## Next steps

Link fabricated parts to exact archive versions. Add original photographs, dimensions, and test records when available.

title: Earn the measurement before making the claim.
summary: A stage-gated plan for turning an assembled low-cost wind tunnel into a characterized low-Reynolds-number instrument, then testing whether dynamic pitch offers a defensible original question. Revised 6 November 2026 after four researcher conversations. No experimental results are claimed.
text:
Can a low-cost, characterized wind-tunnel system reliably quantify aerodynamic-force changes at low Reynolds number — and what changes when angle of attack moves dynamically rather than holding fixed? Advance only when the evidence for the current stage exists: finish and document the instrument; map the empty tunnel; reproduce a fixed-angle NACA 0018 baseline; choose one literature-defined question; cross-check the physics; publish the full record. The sequence is a research design, not a schedule. No measured findings. The conversations changed the plan in three ways: validation comes before novelty, instrument characterization comes before force interpretation, and a dynamic-pitch experiment must pass a mechanical and temporal-response gate before it is treated as feasible. The estimated 50,000–100,000 Reynolds-number range and the verbal “8 by 8” test-section size remain unverified. Interview guidance is not experimental validation. No velocity map, calibration record, force dataset, measured Reynolds number, or confirmed literature gap exists yet. The dynamic-pitch direction, publication path, and mentoring arrangement are not guaranteed. Public attribution of the interviewees still requires confirmation. The original objective was to build an affordable wind tunnel and investigate a conventional airfoil, beginning with NACA 0018. The facility now exists in some form, but the measurement system is unfinished. The interviews made that distinction central.

A fabricated tunnel is an engineering project. A validated instrument is a stronger claim: it produces a measured flow, a documented calibration, and a result another person can inspect. Repeating a well-studied NACA result may establish the second. It does not, by itself, establish a novel contribution.

The revised order is therefore: **characterize, validate, then choose**. The dynamic-angle question remains the preferred exploratory candidate, but only if the apparatus can resolve it without confusing aerodynamics with vibration, sensor lag, or mounting response. | Stage | Objective | Exit evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **01 — Finish the instrument** | Turn the assembled tunnel into a documented measurement system: dimensions, rigid airfoil holder, repeatable angle stand, independent lift and drag channels, calibration references, and a raw-data format. | Dimensioned diagram, wiring schematic, calibration log, data-logging demonstration, and an angle-setting repeatability check. |
| **02 — Characterize the empty tunnel** | Map speed across the test section, quantify variation over time and between runs, and fit control input to measured airspeed rather than trusting fan specifications. | Velocity map, centerline profile, control-to-speed fit with residuals, repeatability plot, and a written uncertainty statement. |
| **03 — Reproduce the NACA 0018 baseline** | Compare fixed-angle lift and drag with published data at the closest achievable Reynolds number, aspect ratio, surface condition, and test geometry. | Coefficient curves with uncertainty, traceable raw data and calculations, and a reasoned account of agreement or disagreement. |
| **04 — Choose one original question** | Use a focused literature review and a feasibility matrix to select one question the apparatus can distinguish from noise, vibration, mounting artifacts, and flow non-uniformity. | A written, cited gap; a comparable-conditions table; and an experimental design that can resolve the expected signal. |
| **05 — Cross-check the physics** | Use CFD or a simpler aerodynamic model to test whether observed trends are plausible after the static baseline is understood — not to certify an uncalibrated instrument. | Documented geometry and boundary conditions, mesh and convergence checks, and a clear account of where the model departs from the experiment. |
| **06 — Publish the record** | Release the protocol, calibration, raw and cleaned data, analysis, null results, and limitations for inspection before pursuing a paper or competition. | A reproducible report and external review. Publication is considered only when the evidence and contribution justify it. |

No stage is complete because time has passed or a part has been built. It is complete when its exit evidence can be inspected. The first two stages are the current work; the later stages remain conditional. | Direction | Motivation from the interviews | Feasibility or novelty condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Transient angle of attack** | Compare the force during motion with the force at the same angle held steady; vary the rate of change. | Controlled actuation, synchronized force/angle/velocity sampling, known sensor bandwidth, and a vibration test that can separate aerodynamic response from mount resonance. |
| **Finite-span / three-dimensional effects** | Study how a real finite wing departs from the two-dimensional assumption behind a NACA section. | Controlled aspect ratio, documented end conditions and wall effects, and a baseline that already agrees with section data. |
| **Morphing or moving geometry** | Examine how a changing surface affects forces over time. | A repeatable mechanism and enough independent measurements to separate geometry, motion rate, and mounting effects. Novelty is not assumed. |
| **Reverse-flow airfoil orientation** | Explore a condition motivated by advancing and retreating rotor-blade aerodynamics. | A confirmed literature gap, controlled orientation, and a test geometry that represents the intended condition. |
| **Measurement-method study** | Use the characterization itself to establish what affordable hardware can and cannot resolve. | A specific methodological comparison, a trusted reference, and an uncertainty analysis strong enough to support a claim about method rather than a single result. |

The current preference is transient angle of attack on a finite NACA 0018 wing. That preference is provisional. A static finite-span comparison or a measurement-method study may be more credible if the dynamic rig cannot separate the expected force change from mechanical response. The plan should change if any of these conditions fails:

- The empty tunnel cannot hold a repeatable speed, or its non-uniformity is too large to assign a defensible Reynolds number.
- The force channels cannot separate lift from drag, or their resolution is too coarse for the loads the airfoil produces.
- A dynamic rig cannot distinguish aerodynamic response from structural vibration, motor noise, or sensor lag.
- The focused literature review finds no gap this apparatus can address.

The response is to improve the instrument or narrow the question, not to reinterpret noise as a result. Negative or inconclusive findings belong in the record when they are honestly measured. 1. Measure the actual test-section geometry and produce a dimensioned diagram. Confirm the units behind the verbal “8 by 8” estimate.
2. Finish the rigid airfoil holder and repeatable angle stand. Record commanded versus measured angle.
3. Run the first empty-tunnel velocity map at several settings, including center, edges, repeats, and stabilization time. The Caltech researcher agreed to serve as a PCIS mentor at approximately one hour per month, with scheduling flexibility. That is conceptual feedback, not sustained hands-on supervision, laboratory placement, authorship, or institutional sponsorship. Publication remains an aspiration rather than a promised deliverable. Public names, titles, and permission to attribute the conversations still need confirmation.

The next review should bring measured characterization evidence and three concrete questions:

1. What minimum velocity-field measurements and uncertainty checks would make this tunnel credible for low-Reynolds-number force measurements?
2. Which published NACA 0018 data are sufficiently similar to the measured operating conditions to serve as a reasonable validation baseline?
3. Would a dynamic-pitch experiment be realistically distinguishable from mechanical vibration and sensor response in this apparatus, or should static finite-span comparisons come first?
